summary: IPsec peers use IKE to negotiate which cryptographic algorithms to use. To keep implementations interoperable, this document gives requirements and guidance on which algorithms IKEv2 implementations must or should support, and it keeps pace with changes in cryptography.

plainLanguage.summary:
IKEv2 is the protocol that two machines use to agree on how to protect the traffic between them. This document says which algorithms every implementation must be able to use, so that two products from different vendors still find common ground.

Each algorithm gets a level. Some must be present, some should be, some are optional, and some are forbidden outright. Algorithms that have started to weaken are moved down rather than removed, so that old and new equipment can still talk to each other while the network moves over.

subtitle: Which cryptographic algorithms an IKEv2 implementation has to have, and which it should drop.

tldr.problem: Two devices running IKEv2 have to agree on which algorithms to use. If each vendor simply supports whatever it likes, two hosts may have nothing in common and the connection fails.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists every algorithm IKEv2 can use and gives each one a requirement level: must, should, may, or must not. It covers encryption, pseudorandom functions, integrity checks, Diffie-Hellman groups and authentication methods, and it calls out separate levels for small devices.
tldr.outcome: Every implementation must support AES-CBC, SHA2-256 based pseudorandom and integrity functions, a 2048-bit Diffie-Hellman group, RSA and shared-key authentication. DES, MD5 and the 768-bit and 1024-bit Diffie-Hellman groups are ruled out. The RFC obsoletes RFC 4307 and has since been updated by RFC 9395.

today: RFC 8247 is a Proposed Standard from September 2017. It obsoletes RFC 4307, updates RFC 7296, and has since been updated by RFC 9395. The document says of itself that new revisions are expected from time to time as best practice changes.

sections.title: Why the Algorithm List Lives in Its Own Document
sections.content:
The Internet Key Exchange protocol is used to negotiate the parameters of the IPsec security association, such as the encryption and authentication algorithms and the keys for the protected communications between the two endpoints. The IKE protocol itself is also protected by cryptographic algorithms, which are negotiated between the two endpoints using IKE. Different implementations of IKE may negotiate different algorithms based on their own local policy, so a set of mandatory-to-implement IKE cryptographic algorithms is defined to ensure interoperability.

This document describes the parameters of the IKE protocol and updates the IKEv2 specification. It changes the mandatory-to-implement authentication algorithms in Section 4 of the IKEv2 specification by saying that RSA key lengths of less than 2048 should not be used. It does not describe the cryptographic parameters of the Authentication Header or Encapsulating Security Payload protocols.

The reason the list sits in a separate document is that cryptography keeps moving. New, stronger algorithms appear and existing ones turn out to be less secure than originally thought, so the requirements have to be updated from time to time. The choices must be conservative to minimize the risk of algorithm compromise, and the algorithms must suit a wide variety of CPU architectures and device deployments, from high-end bulk encryption devices to small low-power devices.

The document also aims to keep implementations interoperable. Interoperability is addressed by introducing or deprecating algorithms incrementally. The mandatory-to-implement algorithm of tomorrow should already be available in most implementations by the time it becomes mandatory, and there is no guarantee that the algorithms in use today will ever become mandatory, because published algorithms are continuously attacked and may become too weak, or completely broken, before the document is updated.

Deprecation is expected to be gradual, which gives implementations time to update while staying interoperable. Unless there are strong security reasons, an algorithm is expected to be downgraded from MUST to MUST- or SHOULD rather than to MUST NOT. Similarly, an algorithm that has not been mentioned as mandatory-to-implement is expected to be introduced with a SHOULD rather than a MUST.

The document gives no recommendations for the use of algorithms, only implementation requirements. The algorithms a particular user chooses are dictated by that user's own security policy, which is outside its scope. IKEv1 is out of scope: it is deprecated, and most IKEv1 implementations have been frozen and cannot update the list.
sections.plainLanguage: The list is separate from the protocol so that it can change without reopening the protocol. The rule of thumb is that weak algorithms are demoted rather than deleted, so that a network does not break on the day the document is updated.

sections.title: What the Requirement Words Mean Here
sections.content:
In the tables in this document the requirement words indicate whether the listed algorithm must, must not, should, should not or may be implemented as part of an IKEv2 implementation. Four additional terms are used.

SHOULD+ means the same as SHOULD, but an algorithm marked this way is likely to be promoted to a MUST at some future time. SHOULD- also means the same as SHOULD, but an algorithm marked this way may be deprecated to a MAY in a future version of the document. MUST- means the same as MUST, but it is expected that the algorithm will no longer be a MUST in a future document; even so, if a future revision changes its status, it is reasonable to expect that it will remain at least a SHOULD or a SHOULD-.

The abbreviation IoT stands for Internet of Things. Requirement levels marked as IoT apply to those devices and to server-side implementations that would presumably need to interoperate with them, including any general-purpose VPN gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: The plus and minus signs are warnings. A plus means an algorithm is on its way up and a minus means it is on its way down, so implementers know which way to plan.

sections.title: The Four Kinds of Algorithm
sections.content:
IKEv2 negotiates four kinds of algorithm. The first is the encryption algorithm, negotiated in the security association payload and used for the encrypted payload. Some of them are authenticated encryption with associated data; algorithms that are not must be used together with one of the integrity algorithms.

For encryption, ENCR_AES_CBC is raised from SHOULD+ for 128-bit keys and MAY for 256-bit keys in the earlier list to MUST, with 192-bit keys remaining at MAY. It is the only algorithm mandatory in both this document and the earlier one, which is why it is needed for interoperability with an implementation compatible with that earlier list. ENCR_CHACHA20_POLY1305 is recommended by the IRTF cryptography forum as an alternative to AES-CBC and AES-GCM; at the time of writing there were not enough IKEv2 implementations supporting it to introduce it at the SHOULD+ level. ENCR_AES_GCM_16 was not considered in the earlier list, because AES-GCM was then defined only for ESP and later for IKEv2. Its main motivation for ESP was encryption performance compared with AES-CBC, which led to wide implementation for ESP; but the computation load of IKEv2 is small compared with ESP, so many IKEv2 implementations had not implemented AES-GCM, and it is not promoted beyond SHOULD. The reason for the promotion from MAY is to favour the slightly more secure authenticated method over the traditional encrypt-and-authenticate method. The 8-octet and 12-octet check values remain at MAY because the advantage of the shorter and weaker values is minimal.

ENCR_AES_CCM_8 is not considered in the earlier list, and is listed as SHOULD so that implementations can interact with IoT devices. The 8-octet size of the check value is expected to be sufficient for most IKEv2 use cases, since far fewer packets are exchanged there and IoT devices want packets as small as possible; the level applies to 128-bit keys, with 256-bit keys at MAY. ENCR_3DES is downgraded from MUST- to MAY, because every IKEv2 implementation already has AES-CBC and there is no need to keep the much slower algorithm. ENCR_DES can be brute-forced using off-the-shelf hardware and provides no meaningful security, so it must not be implemented. ENCR_NULL was wrongly specified as MAY in the earlier list, even though the IKEv2 specification clearly states that it must not be used.

The second kind is the pseudorandom function, used to generate pseudorandom values when needed. PRF_HMAC_SHA2_256 must be implemented, to replace SHA1 and the SHA1-based function, since no SHA2-based transforms were referenced in the earlier list. PRF_HMAC_SHA2_512 should be implemented as a future replacement or when stronger security is required, and is preferred over the 384-bit version because the extra overhead is negligible. PRF_HMAC_SHA1 is downgraded from MUST to MUST-, because attacks against SHA1 are increasing and there is an industry-wide trend to deprecate it. PRF_AES128_XCBC is recommended only for IoT, where deployments prefer AES-based functions to avoid implementing SHA2; for ordinary VPN deployment it is downgraded from SHOULD to MAY, as it has not seen wide adoption. PRF_HMAC_MD5 is downgraded from MAY to MUST NOT.

The third kind is the integrity algorithm, negotiated in the security association payload and used for the encrypted payload. When an authenticated encryption algorithm is proposed, this transform type is not in use. AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_256_128 must be implemented to replace the SHA1-based function. AUTH_HMAC_SHA2_512_256 should be implemented as a future replacement or when stronger security is required. AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96 is downgraded to MUST-. AUTH_AES_XCBC_96 is recommended only for IoT and is downgraded from SHOULD to MAY for ordinary VPN deployment. AUTH_DES_MAC and AUTH_KPDK_MD5, which were not mentioned in the earlier list and so defaulted to MAY, are downgraded to MUST NOT, along with AUTH_HMAC_MD5_96.

The fourth kind is the Diffie-Hellman group. The exchange has to be enforced securely because it produces the keys for the session: an attacker who retrieves one private number and the complementary public value can compute the secret, and such an attack can be performed offline on a recorded communication years later. Group 14, the 2048-bit MODP group, is raised from SHOULD+ to MUST as a replacement for the 1024-bit group, and is widely implemented and considered secure. Group 19, the 256-bit random elliptic curve group, was not defined at the time of the earlier list and is promoted to SHOULD. Group 5, the 1536-bit group, is downgraded to SHOULD NOT because it is considered vulnerable to being broken within the next few years by a nation-state-level attack. Group 2, the 1024-bit group, is downgraded to SHOULD NOT, being weak against sufficiently funded attackers using commercially available mass-computing resources, and is expected to be downgraded to MUST NOT in the near future. Group 1, the 768-bit group, can be broken within hours using cheap off-the-shelf hardware and provides no security whatsoever, so it is downgraded to MUST NOT.

Groups 22, 23 and 24 are MODP groups with prime order subgroups that are not safe primes. Their seeds have not been publicly released, which has reduced trust in them, and they were proposed as alternatives for groups 2 and 14 but never saw wide deployment. Group 22 with 1024-bit MODP has been shown to be too weak, and academia has the resources to generate malicious values at that size, so it is demoted to MUST NOT. Groups 23 and 24 are demoted to SHOULD NOT and are expected to be downgraded further, and because they have small subgroups the additional checks of the IKEv2 Diffie-Hellman tests must be done when they are used.
sections.plainLanguage: IKEv2 needs four things: a way to encrypt, a way to generate random-looking values, a way to check that nothing was tampered with, and a way to agree on a shared secret. The tables say which choice of each is mandatory and which is on the way out.

sections.title: What Changed From the Earlier List
sections.content: The RFC closes with a table summarising the changes from the earlier list. ENCR_3DES moves from MUST- to MAY. ENCR_NULL stays MUST NOT, after an erratum corrected the earlier list. ENCR_AES_CBC moves from SHOULD+ to MUST. ENCR_AES_CTR moves from SHOULD to MAY, because the algorithm is not mentioned in the sections of this document and so defaults to MAY. PRF_HMAC_MD5 moves from MAY to MUST NOT. PRF_HMAC_SHA1 moves from MUST to MUST-. PRF_AES128_XCBC moves from SHOULD+ to SHOULD. AUTH_HMAC_MD5_96 moves from MAY to MUST NOT. AUTH_HMAC_SHA1_96 moves from MUST to MUST-. AUTH_AES_XCBC_96 moves from SHOULD+ to SHOULD. Group 2, the 1024-bit group, moves from MUST- to SHOULD NOT, and group 14, the 2048-bit group, moves from SHOULD+ to MUST.
sections.plainLanguage: The short version: AES-CBC and the 2048-bit group were promoted, the SHA1 and MD5 algorithms were demoted, and 3DES was let go of.

sections.title: Authentication Methods and Key Lengths
sections.content:
IKEv2 authentication may involve verifying signatures. Signatures may be used to validate a certificate or to check the signature of the AUTH value. Cryptographic recommendations about certificate validation are out of scope, because what is mandatory to implement there is provided by the PKIX community; this document is mostly concerned with signature verification and generation.

For authentication methods, RSA Digital Signature is widely deployed and so is kept for interoperability, although it is expected to be downgraded in the future, since its signatures are based on the older RSASSA-PKCS1-v1.5, which is no longer recommended. RSA authentication and other specific methods are expected to be replaced by the generic Digital Signature method. Shared Key Message Integrity Code is widely deployed and has always been mandatory, so its status remains MUST. DSS Digital Signature is bound to SHA-1 and has the same level of security as 1024-bit RSA; it is at SHOULD NOT and expected to be downgraded to MUST NOT. The elliptic curve methods are expected to be downgraded too, since they do not provide hash function agility, so ECDSA is expected to be performed through the generic Digital Signature method instead; its status is SHOULD. The generic Digital Signature method is expected to be promoted, because it provides hash function, signature format and algorithm agility, and its current status is SHOULD.

For RSA key lengths, a key length of 2048 is MUST, key lengths of 3072 and 4096 are SHOULD, key lengths between 2049 and 4095 are MAY, and key lengths smaller than 2048 are SHOULD NOT. The IKEv2 specification mandates support for RSA keys of 1024 or 2048 bits, but the smaller size is downgraded because there is an industry-wide trend to deprecate key lengths below 2048 bits. Since these signatures only have value in real time and need no future protection, the smaller key was kept at SHOULD NOT rather than MUST NOT.

When the generic Digital Signature method is implemented, the hash function recommendations apply: SHA1 is MUST NOT, SHA2-256 is MUST, SHA2-384 is MAY and SHA2-512 is SHOULD. When it is used with the RSA signature algorithm, RSASSA-PSS must be supported and RSASSA-PKCS1-v1.5 may be supported. The table in the generic notation adds that RSASSA-PSS with SHA-256 is MUST, ecdsa-with-sha256 is SHOULD, and that sha1WithRSAEncryption, dsa-with-sha1 and ecdsa-with-sha1 are all MUST NOT, as are RSASSA-PSS with empty or default parameters, since those mean SHA1.
sections.plainLanguage: Two ways of proving who you are must be supported: a signature with an RSA key, and a shared secret. The RSA key must be at least 2048 bits, and the older 1024-bit size is discouraged but not forbidden, because signatures do not need to stay verifiable for ever.

sections.title: Algorithms for Small Devices
sections.content:
Several algorithms in the document are marked for use with the Internet of Things, for several reasons. IoT devices are usually very constrained, with so little memory and CPU power that these clients only have the resources to implement and run one set of algorithms. For example, instead of implementing both AES and SHA, these devices typically use the AES-XCBC integrity algorithm so that SHA does not have to be implemented.

Devices following the IEEE 802.15.4 standard have a mandatory-to-implement link-level security using AES-CCM with 128-bit keys, and the recommended practice for transporting key management protocol datagrams already provides a way to use Minimal IKEv2 over that layer to provide link keys. Such devices might want to use AES-CCM as their IKEv2 algorithm so that they can reuse the hardware implementing it. They cannot use AES-CBC, because the hardware quite often does not include the AES decryption needed for CBC mode, so despite AES-CCM requiring authenticated encryption support, reusing the crypto hardware makes it the preferred algorithm.

Another important aspect is that the transfer rates of such devices are usually quite low, in the order of tens of kbit/s, and each bit transmitted has an energy cost that shortens battery life, so shorter packets are preferred. That is the reason for recommending the 8-octet check value over the 16-octet one.

Because different IoT devices have different constraints, the document cannot specify the one mandatory profile for IoT. Instead it points out the commonly used algorithms.
sections.plainLanguage: A tiny sensor cannot afford to implement several different algorithms, and its radio chip may already contain exactly one of them. The recommendations point at the ones that match that hardware, and prefer shorter messages because every bit costs battery life.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of cryptographic-based systems depends on both the strength of the algorithms chosen and the strength of the keys used with them. It also depends on the engineering of the protocol to ensure that there are no non-cryptographic ways to bypass the security of the overall system.

The Diffie-Hellman group parameter is the most important one to choose conservatively. Any party that captures all the IKE and ESP traffic and can later break the selected group in IKE can gain access to the symmetric keys used to encrypt all the ESP traffic, so these groups must be chosen very conservatively. However, specifying an extremely large group also puts a considerable load on the device, especially a large VPN gateway or an IoT-constrained device.

The algorithms identified in this document as MUST or SHOULD implement are not known to be broken at the current time, and cryptographic research so far suggests they are likely to remain secure into the foreseeable future. This is not necessarily forever, and it is expected that new revisions of the document will be issued from time to time to reflect the current best practice.
sections.plainLanguage: The group used to agree on a shared secret matters more than anything else in this list, because breaking it later on a recorded conversation is enough to unlock everything. But a very large group costs the device a lot of work, so there is a trade-off.

viz.caption: The IKEv2 encryption algorithms and their levels

items.label: MUST
items.desc: For 128-bit and 256-bit keys. The only algorithm mandatory in both this list and the earlier one.

items.label: SHOULD
items.desc: An authenticated encryption method. Not promoted further because many IKEv2 implementations had not implemented it.

items.label: SHOULD
items.desc: An authenticated encryption method, recommended by the IRTF cryptography forum as an alternative to AES.

items.label: SHOULD
items.desc: For interoperability with small devices. Only 128-bit keys are at this level.

items.label: MAY
items.desc: Demoted, because every IKEv2 implementation already has AES-CBC and 3DES is much slower.

items.label: MUST NOT
items.desc: Can be brute-forced with off-the-shelf hardware and provides no meaningful security.

items.label: MUST NOT
items.desc: Already forbidden by the IKEv2 specification; the earlier list wrongly made it optional.

viz.caption: The Diffie-Hellman groups and their levels

items.label: MUST
items.desc: The 2048-bit MODP group, raised from SHOULD+ in the earlier list as a replacement for the 1024-bit group.

items.label: SHOULD
items.desc: The 256-bit random elliptic curve group, which was not defined at the time of the earlier list.

items.label: SHOULD NOT
items.desc: The 1536-bit MODP group, considered vulnerable to being broken within a few years by a nation-state-level attack.

items.label: SHOULD NOT
items.desc: The 1024-bit MODP group, weak against well-funded attackers using commercially available mass computing.

items.label: MUST NOT
items.desc: The 768-bit MODP group, which can be broken within hours using cheap off-the-shelf hardware.

items.label: MUST NOT
items.desc: 1024-bit MODP with a 160-bit prime order subgroup, which has been shown to be too weak.

items.label: SHOULD NOT
items.desc: 2048-bit MODP groups with small subgroups, whose seeds were never publicly released.

viz.caption: The IKEv2 authentication methods and their levels

items.label: MUST
items.desc: RSA digital signature, kept because it is widely deployed.

items.label: MUST
items.desc: Shared key message integrity code, which has always been mandatory.

items.label: SHOULD NOT
items.desc: DSS digital signature, bound to SHA-1 and of the same strength as 1024-bit RSA.

items.label: SHOULD
items.desc: ECDSA with SHA-256 on the P-256 curve, SHA-384 on P-384 and SHA-512 on P-521.

items.label: SHOULD
items.desc: The generic digital signature method, which offers hash and algorithm agility.

viz.caption: How the requirement levels moved from the earlier list
The requirement levels used in the tables

items.title: MUST
items.text: Every implementation must have this algorithm.

items.title: SHOULD+
items.text: Should be implemented, and is likely to become a MUST later.

items.title: SHOULD-
items.text: Should be implemented, and may be downgraded to optional later.

items.title: MUST-
items.text: Must be implemented, but is expected to stop being mandatory later, and will at least remain optional.

viz.caption: Why small devices want different algorithms

items.title: One set of algorithms only
items.text: Small devices have the memory and CPU for a single set of algorithms and no more.

items.title: Reuse the hardware
items.text: A device whose radio chip does AES-CCM cannot use AES-CBC, because the hardware often lacks AES decryption, so AES-CCM is preferred despite needing authenticated encryption support.

items.title: Shorter packets
items.text: Transfer rates are in the order of tens of kbit/s and every bit costs battery life, so the 8-octet check value is preferred over the 16-octet one.

items.title: No single profile
items.text: Because the constraints differ from device to device, the document points out commonly used algorithms rather than mandating one profile.
